title: Easy exam 2
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: one concept each, with the classic look-alike options.

questions.title: Owner with write permission only
questions.text: You own `data.txt`, a regular file whose mode is `--w-------`. What does `cat data.txt` do?

options.t: It prints the contents, because the owner of a file can always read it.
options.why: Being the owner gives no permission by itself: the bits decide, and `r` is missing.

options.t: It fails with `Permission denied`: reading needs `r` and the file only has `w`.
options.why: `cat` must read the file; `w` alone does not allow it (appending with `>>` would work).

options.t: It prints nothing and ends successfully, because a write-only file shows nothing.
options.why: `cat` reports an error and returns a non-zero status; it does not silently succeed.

options.t: It prints the contents, because `cat` only needs `x` or `w` on the file to open it.
options.why: Reading needs `r`; `x` is for running the file and `w` for changing it.

questions.title: Builtin or external
questions.text: Which statement about builtin and external commands is FALSE?

options.t: To run a builtin such as `jobs`, the shell searches `PATH` for an executable file called `jobs`.
options.why: False: a builtin is implemented inside the shell, so no file is searched for or started.

options.t: `ls` and `cp` are external commands: each is a program file that the shell finds through `PATH`.
options.why: True: they are programs on disk, for example `/usr/bin/ls`.

options.t: `type cd` answers that `cd` is a shell builtin.
options.why: True: `type` tells how the shell would interpret a name.

options.t: `whereis ls` shows the path of the executable of `ls` and of its manual pages.
options.why: True: it prints entries such as `/usr/bin/ls` and `/usr/share/man/man1/ls.1.gz`.

questions.title: Adding a user to a group
questions.text: On a Debian-like system the user `marta` and the group `lab` already exist. Which command makes `marta` a member of `lab`?

options.t: `addgroup lab marta`
options.why: `addgroup` creates groups; with two arguments it refuses ("unspecified operation").

options.t: `deluser marta lab`
options.why: It does the opposite: it removes `marta` from the group `lab`.

options.t: `adduser marta lab`
options.why: `adduser user group` adds an existing user to an existing group.

options.t: `adduser lab marta`
options.why: The arguments are in the wrong order: it looks for a user called `lab`, which does not exist.

questions.title: Aliases
questions.text: Which statement about aliases in bash is TRUE?

options.t: `unalias ll` deletes the program called `ll` from the disk.
options.why: It only removes the alias from the current shell; no file is touched.

options.t: An alias typed at the prompt is saved automatically and is available in every terminal opened later.
options.why: To keep it you have to write it in a startup file such as `~/.bashrc`.

options.t: `alias` with no arguments deletes all the aliases of the session.
options.why: With no arguments it lists the aliases that are defined.

options.t: After `alias ll='ls -l'`, typing `ll /tmp` runs `ls -l /tmp`.
options.why: The shell replaces the first word with the alias text and keeps the rest of the line.

questions.title: Fields with cut
questions.text: `echo 'tea,milk,rice,salt' | cut -d, -f2,4` is run. Which statement is FALSE?

options.t: The output is `milk salt`: `cut` joins the fields with a space.
options.why: False: `cut` keeps the input delimiter, so the output is `milk,salt`.

options.t: `cut -d, -f3` on the same line prints `rice`.
options.why: True: `-f3` selects the third field.

options.t: `cut -d, -f2-3` on the same line prints `milk,rice`, the second and third fields.
options.why: True: a range selects consecutive fields and keeps the delimiter between them.

options.t: `cut -c5-8` on the same line prints `milk`, characters 5 to 8 of the line.
options.why: True: `-c` selects characters by position; characters 5 to 8 are `milk`.

questions.title: UEFI and legacy BIOS
questions.text: Which statement about UEFI and the legacy BIOS is TRUE?

options.t: UEFI is the older firmware, and the BIOS replaced it by adding Secure Boot.
options.why: It is the other way round: UEFI is the successor of the BIOS.

options.t: UEFI replaces the BIOS and can work with GPT disks and offer Secure Boot.
options.why: Secure Boot lets the firmware refuse boot software that is not signed.

options.t: UEFI only boots from MBR disks, while GPT disks are used only by the legacy BIOS.
options.why: Swapped: GPT is the partition table that goes with UEFI, and MBR with the BIOS.

options.t: Secure Boot encrypts the disk, so its files cannot be read without the owner's password.
options.why: Secure Boot checks signatures of the boot software; it does not encrypt anything.

questions.title: Default streams
questions.text: Which line describes correctly where the three standard streams of a command go by default when it is run at a terminal?

options.t: stdin (0) is read from the file named in the first argument, stdout (1) goes to the screen and stderr (2) goes to the screen.
options.why: Without `<`, stdin is the keyboard; a file argument is something the command itself opens.

options.t: stdin (0) is the keyboard, stdout (1) goes to the screen and stderr (2) is discarded unless it is redirected.
options.why: Errors are not discarded: stderr also goes to the screen by default.

options.t: stdin (1) is the keyboard, stdout (0) goes to the screen and stderr (2) goes to the screen.
options.why: The numbers are swapped: 0 is stdin and 1 is stdout.

options.t: stdin (0) is the keyboard, and both stdout (1) and stderr (2) go to the screen.
options.why: Both outputs go to the terminal unless redirected, which is why `2>` is useful to separate the errors.

questions.title: rmdir after mkdir -p
questions.text: In an empty directory you run `mkdir -p a/b` and then `rmdir a`. What happens?

options.t: Both `a` and `b` are removed, because `b` is empty and `rmdir` removes a directory with its empty subdirectories.
options.why: `rmdir` only removes the directory it is given, and only if that one is empty.

options.t: `rmdir` asks for confirmation and removes `a` with `b` inside it if you answer `y`.
options.why: `rmdir` never asks; deleting a directory with content needs `rm -r`.

options.t: `rmdir` fails with "Directory not empty", because `a` still contains `b`.
options.why: `-p` of `mkdir` created both levels; `rmdir` removes only empty directories and `a` holds `b`.

options.t: Only `a` is removed, and `b` stays in the current directory.
options.why: Nothing is moved; the command fails and both directories remain.

questions.title: Copying with -u
questions.text: `src/notes.txt` is older than `dest/notes.txt`. What does `cp -u src/notes.txt dest/` do?

options.t: It overwrites `dest/notes.txt` with the old file, because `-u` means "unconditional".
options.why: `-u` means "update": it copies only when the source is newer or the destination is missing.

options.t: It asks `overwrite 'dest/notes.txt'?` and waits for `y` or `n`.
options.why: That is `-i` (interactive).

options.t: It keeps both versions: the old one is saved as `notes.txt~` and the source is copied.
options.why: Backups need `-b`; `-u` does not create any.

options.t: It does nothing: the destination is newer, so it is left untouched.
options.why: `-u` skips the copy when the destination is at least as recent as the source.

questions.title: Environment after running a script
questions.text: `setup.sh` contains the single line `export MODE=test`, and it has execute permission. Which statement is TRUE?

options.t: After `./setup.sh`, `echo $MODE` prints `test`, because the variable was exported.
options.why: `./setup.sh` runs in a child shell; `export` passes the variable only to that child's own children, never back to the parent.

options.t: After `. setup.sh`, `echo $MODE` prints `test` in your current shell.
options.why: `.` (same as `source`) runs the lines in the current shell, so the variable stays.

options.t: After `bash setup.sh`, `echo $MODE` prints `test`, because `bash` runs the script with the current environment.
options.why: It starts a new shell: the variable disappears when it ends.

options.t: After `. setup.sh`, `echo $MODE` prints nothing, because `.` runs the script in a child shell.
options.why: `.` does not create a child; that is what `./` and `bash` do.
